findings.text: AI21 reports safety metrics similar to those in the literature and points to an alignment section rather than a risk-threshold framework.

source.quote:
We also observe similar safety metrics as those reported in the literature. We refer to
Section 7 for more information about our general approach for safety and alignment of models.

findings.text: Alignment is organized around OECD AI principles, with 60 behavioral tenets stated as directives of behavior for models to avoid; the full list was to be made public.

source.quote:
In total, we have created 60 tenets that map to the OECD principles. These tenets are stated as
directives of behavior for our models to avoid. The full list will be made publicly available.

findings.text: AI21 cites engagement with OECD, Stanford [HELM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110), and Foundation Model Transparency Index (FMTI), and a 2nd-place FMTI ranking as of May 2024, as accountability/transparency rather than third-party safety tests of these models.

source.quote:
Our engagement with OECD, Stanford’s HELM [23] and FMTI [3] and
documents like this demonstrate this commitment, as well as our high ranking on the FMTI (2nd as
of May 2024).

findings.text: The authors found proximal policy optimization (PPO)/direct preference optimization (DPO) preference tuning helpful for alignment with human intent, but careful synthetic data, filtering, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) were crucial for a strong post-trained model.

source.quote:
Finally, while preference tuning algorithms like PPO [33] or DPO [29] improve alignment between
model outputs and human intent, we found that the combination of careful synthetic data generation,
data filtering, and supervised fine-tuning is crucial for obtaining a strong post-trained model.
